MAT.author: the apostle Matthew (Levi), a former tax collector
MAT.audience: Jewish Christians (traditionally in Palestine or Syria)
MAT.setting: Written in a Jewish-Christian setting before the fall of Jerusalem in A.D. 70, as the church was defining itself over against the synagogue.
MAT.theme: Jesus the Messiah, the promised King of the Jews
MAT.summary: Matthew, one of the Twelve, wrote to show that Jesus of Nazareth is the long-promised Messiah, the Son of David and heir of Abraham. He repeatedly cites the Old Testament ("that it might be fulfilled") and gathers Jesus' teaching into five great discourses, beginning with the Sermon on the Mount. The Gospel traces the King's offer of the kingdom of heaven, His rejection by Israel's leaders, and His death and resurrection, closing with the Great Commission to make disciples of all nations.
MAT.christ: Jesus is the royal Messiah, Son of David and Son of God, who fulfills the Law and the Prophets and to whom all power in heaven and in earth is given.

outline.title: The King's genealogy, birth, and infancy
The King prepared: John, baptism, and temptation
Ministry begins; the Sermon on the Mount
The King's power: miracles and the sending of the Twelve
Growing opposition and the parables of the kingdom
Training the disciples: Peter's confession and the church
The King in Jerusalem: entry, conflict, and the Olivet Discourse
The King's death and resurrection; the Great Commission

MRK.author: John Mark, Peter's companion and interpreter
MRK.setting: Traditionally written in Rome from Peter's preaching, for Gentile believers facing hardship and the threat of persecution.
MRK.theme: Jesus the Servant Son of God, who gives His life a ransom
MRK.summary: Early tradition (Papias) holds that Mark, a companion of both Peter and Paul, wrote down Peter's preaching about Jesus. The shortest and most action-filled Gospel, it moves quickly ("straightway") from one deed to the next and explains Jewish customs for Gentile readers. Its first half displays Jesus' authority over disease, demons, nature, and death; from Peter's confession onward it turns toward the cross, where the Servant gives His life a ransom for many.
MRK.christ: Jesus is the mighty Son of God who came not to be ministered unto but to minister, and to give His life a ransom for many.

outline.title: The Twelve, the parables, and mighty works
Peter's confession and the road to Jerusalem
Ministry in Jerusalem and the Olivet Discourse
The Servant's betrayal, trial, and crucifixion

LUK.author: Luke, the beloved physician and companion of Paul
LUK.setting: Written for a Greek-speaking, largely Gentile readership, probably while Paul was in custody at Caesarea or Rome.
LUK.theme: Jesus the Son of Man, Savior of the lost
LUK.summary: Luke, a Gentile physician and Paul's traveling companion, carefully investigated eyewitness accounts to write an orderly narrative for Theophilus. His Gospel, the first volume of a two-part work with Acts, contains much material found nowhere else, including the births of John and Jesus and parables such as the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son. Luke stresses prayer, the Holy Spirit, joy, and Jesus' compassion for the poor, women, Samaritans, and outcasts, presenting a Savior for all people.
LUK.christ: Jesus is the perfect Son of Man and Savior of the world, who came to seek and to save that which was lost.

outline.title: Births of John and Jesus; Jesus' childhood
The Son of Man betrayed and crucified

JHN.author: the apostle John
JHN.audience: believers and seekers in the wider church (traditionally from Ephesus)
JHN.setting: Written late in the first century, traditionally at Ephesus, after the other Gospels were circulating and as the church faced false teaching and opposition from the synagogue.
JHN.theme: Believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life
JHN.summary: John, "the disciple whom Jesus loved," wrote the fourth Gospel late in life, supplementing the other three with material largely unique to it. He selects a series of signs and records extended discourses, including the great "I am" sayings, to show that Jesus is the eternal Word made flesh. He states his purpose plainly: that readers might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life through His name.
JHN.christ: Jesus is the eternal Word, God made flesh, the only begotten Son who reveals the Father and gives eternal life to all who believe.

outline.title: The Son's claims and growing conflict
The Upper Room: farewell discourse and prayer

ACT.author: Luke, the beloved physician
ACT.setting: Spans about thirty years, from the ascension (c. A.D. 30) to Paul's two years under house arrest in Rome, where the book ends.
ACT.theme: The risen Christ spreads His gospel by the Spirit to the ends of the earth
ACT.summary: Acts continues Luke's Gospel, recording what Jesus continued to do and teach through His apostles by the Holy Spirit. Beginning with the ascension and Pentecost, it traces the gospel's spread from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and on to the Gentile world, following first Peter and then Paul. It records the founding of the church, the conversion of Saul, the Jerusalem Council, and Paul's missionary journeys, ending with Paul preaching the kingdom of God unhindered in Rome.
ACT.christ: The ascended Lord Jesus pours out the promised Spirit and builds His church, proclaimed as the only name under heaven whereby we must be saved.

outline.title: The ascension and waiting for the Spirit
Pentecost and the church in Jerusalem
Samaria, Saul's conversion, and the first Gentiles

ROM.author: the apostle Paul
ROM.audience: the church at Rome, Jews and Gentiles
ROM.setting: Written from Corinth near the end of the third missionary journey, as Paul prepared to carry the collection to Jerusalem and hoped to visit Rome on his way to Spain.
ROM.theme: The righteousness of God revealed in the gospel
ROM.summary: Romans is Paul's fullest and most systematic presentation of the gospel. He shows that Jews and Gentiles alike stand guilty before God, that sinners are justified freely by grace through faith in Christ's atoning work, and that the justified are freed from sin's dominion to live by the Spirit. He then addresses God's sovereign purposes for Israel and closes with practical instruction on living sacrifice, love, civil authority, and the unity of strong and weak believers.
ROM.christ: Christ is the Son of God, declared with power by the resurrection, set forth as a propitiation through faith in His blood and raised again for our justification.

outline.title: Sanctification: freedom from sin and life in the Spirit

1CO.author: the apostle Paul
1CO.setting: Written from Ephesus during the third missionary journey to a young church in Corinth, a wealthy, cosmopolitan, and notoriously immoral Greek port city.
1CO.theme: Correcting a divided church and answering its questions
1CO.summary: Paul had founded the church at Corinth on his second missionary journey, and later reports and a letter from the church revealed serious problems. He confronts factions, tolerated immorality, lawsuits among believers, and disorder at the Lord's Supper, and answers questions about marriage, food offered to idols, spiritual gifts, and the resurrection. Throughout, he applies the wisdom of the cross and the law of love to the life of a worldly congregation.
1CO.christ: Christ crucified is the power and wisdom of God, the one foundation of the church, and the firstfruits of the resurrection.

outline.title: Divisions and the wisdom of the cross
Christian liberty and food offered to idols

2CO.author: the apostle Paul (with Timothy)
2CO.audience: the church at Corinth and the saints in Achaia
2CO.setting: Written from Macedonia after Titus brought news of Corinth's response to Paul's severe letter, while false apostles still challenged his authority.
2CO.theme: God's power made perfect in weakness
2CO.summary: After a painful visit and a severe letter, Paul rejoiced at Titus's report that most of the Corinthians had repented, yet some, stirred up by self-styled apostles, still attacked his ministry. This is Paul's most personal letter, opening his heart about his sufferings, motives, and calling as a minister of the new covenant. He urges completion of the collection for the poor saints in Jerusalem and defends his apostleship by glorying in his infirmities, through which Christ's power is displayed.
2CO.christ: Christ is the One in whom all God's promises are yea and amen, who became poor for our sakes and was made sin for us that we might be made the righteousness of God in Him.

outline.title: The ministry of the new covenant

GAL.author: the apostle Paul
GAL.setting: Written to churches founded by Paul, as Judaizing teachers pressed Gentile converts to be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses.
GAL.theme: Justification by faith alone and freedom in Christ
GAL.summary: Soon after Paul evangelized Galatia, teachers arrived insisting that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the Law to be accepted by God. Paul responds with urgency, defending his apostolic authority as received directly from Christ and showing from Abraham's example that justification has always been by faith. He concludes that believers are free from the Law's bondage, yet called to use that liberty to serve one another by walking in the Spirit.
GAL.christ: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, being made a curse for us, and lives in those who are crucified with Him.

outline.title: Justification by faith, not by the Law
Liberty in Christ and life in the Spirit

EPH.author: the apostle Paul
EPH.audience: the saints at Ephesus (likely also circulated in Asia)
EPH.setting: Written during Paul's first Roman imprisonment and carried by Tychicus, together with Colossians and Philemon.
EPH.theme: The believer's riches in Christ and the unity of His church
EPH.summary: Ephesians, written from prison and lacking personal greetings, may have been intended to circulate among the churches of Asia. Its first three chapters unfold the believer's spiritual blessings in Christ: election, redemption, and adoption; salvation by grace through faith; and the union of Jew and Gentile in one body. Its last three chapters call the church to walk worthy of that calling in unity, purity, and love, in the home, and in spiritual warfare.
EPH.christ: Christ is the exalted Head over all things to the church, who has made Jew and Gentile one new man and loves the church as His bride.

outline.title: Spiritual blessings in Christ and Paul's prayer
Saved by grace and made one in Christ
The mystery revealed and Paul's prayer
The whole armour of God; closing

PHP.author: the apostle Paul (with Timothy)
PHP.setting: Written from imprisonment, traditionally Paul's first Roman imprisonment, to thank the Philippians for the gift brought by Epaphroditus.
PHP.theme: Joy in Christ in every circumstance
PHP.summary: The church at Philippi, the first Paul founded in Europe, had faithfully supported him and sent Epaphroditus with a gift while he was imprisoned. Paul writes to thank them, report on his circumstances, and urge them toward unity and humility after the example of Christ. Though in bonds and facing possible death, he speaks repeatedly of joy, warns against the Judaizers, and testifies that he has learned contentment through Christ who strengthens him.
PHP.christ: Christ is the eternal Son who, being in the form of God, humbled Himself unto the death of the cross and has been highly exalted as Lord over all.

outline.title: Paul's circumstances: to live is Christ
The mind of Christ: humility and service
Knowing Christ: no confidence in the flesh
Peace, contentment, and thanks for the gift

COL.author: the apostle Paul (with Timothy)
COL.setting: Written from Paul's first Roman imprisonment after Epaphras reported a false teaching that mixed philosophy, Jewish ritual, and the worship of angels.
COL.theme: The preeminence and sufficiency of Christ
COL.summary: Paul had not visited Colossae; the church was founded through Epaphras, who brought word of a dangerous teaching combining human philosophy, Jewish ritual, asceticism, and the worship of angels. Paul answers it by exalting Christ as the image of the invisible God, the Creator and Head of the church, in whom dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. Since believers are complete in Him, they need no additions, but are to set their affection on things above and live out their new life in every relationship.
COL.christ: Christ is the image of the invisible God, Creator and upholder of all things, the Head of the church, in whom dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily.

outline.title: The preeminence of Christ and Paul's ministry
Complete in Christ: warning against false teaching

1TH.author: the apostle Paul (with Silas and Timothy)
1TH.setting: Written from Corinth during the second missionary journey, after Timothy brought good news of the young and persecuted church.
1TH.theme: Faithful, holy living in hope of the Lord's coming
1TH.summary: Paul founded the church at Thessalonica on his second journey but was forced to leave after a short time because of persecution. Anxious about the new believers, he sent Timothy, whose report of their faith and love prompted this warm letter. Paul recalls his conduct among them, urges holiness and quiet diligence, and comforts those grieving over believers who had died by teaching about the Lord's coming and the resurrection.
1TH.christ: Jesus is the risen Son who delivers us from the wrath to come and will descend from heaven to gather His people to Himself.

2TH.author: the apostle Paul (with Silas and Timothy)
2TH.setting: Written from Corinth shortly after 1 Thessalonians, to correct the mistaken idea that the day of Christ had already come.
2TH.theme: Steadfastness until the day of the Lord
2TH.summary: Persecution at Thessalonica continued, and some had been shaken by a report, perhaps even a forged letter, claiming that the day of Christ was already present. Paul comforts them with the certainty of God's righteous judgment at Christ's return and explains that the falling away and the revealing of the man of sin must come first. He also rebukes those who had stopped working, commanding them to work quietly and eat their own bread.
2TH.christ: The Lord Jesus will be revealed from heaven in flaming fire to take vengeance on the disobedient and be glorified in His saints, consuming the man of sin with the brightness of His coming.

outline.title: The day of Christ and the man of sin
Prayer, discipline of the disorderly, and closing

1TI.author: the apostle Paul
1TI.audience: Timothy, Paul's son in the faith, at Ephesus
1TI.setting: Written after Paul's release from his first Roman imprisonment, during a further period of ministry not recorded in Acts.
1TI.theme: Sound doctrine and godly order in the house of God
1TI.summary: Paul had left Timothy at Ephesus to oppose false teachers and set the church in order. This letter gives instruction on prayer and public worship, the qualifications of bishops and deacons, the care of widows, the honor due to elders, and the dangers of the love of money. Paul urges his young delegate to guard sound doctrine, be an example to the believers, and fight the good fight of faith.
1TI.christ: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; He is the one Mediator between God and men, God manifest in the flesh.

outline.title: Warning against false teachers; Paul's testimony
A good minister of Jesus Christ
False teachers, riches, and a final charge

2TI.author: the apostle Paul
2TI.audience: Timothy, Paul's son in the faith
2TI.setting: Paul's final letter, written from a Roman prison shortly before his martyrdom under Nero.
2TI.theme: Faithfulness to the gospel to the end
2TI.summary: Imprisoned again in Rome, deserted by many, and expecting execution, Paul wrote his last letter to Timothy, his dearly beloved son. He urges Timothy not to be ashamed of the gospel, to endure hardness as a good soldier, and to commit the truth to faithful men. Warning of perilous times and departure from the truth, he affirms that all Scripture is given by inspiration of God and charges Timothy to preach the word, asking him to come before winter.
2TI.christ: Christ Jesus has abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel; He is the righteous Judge who will give the crown of righteousness.

outline.title: A good soldier of Jesus Christ
Perilous times and the sufficiency of Scripture

TIT.author: the apostle Paul
TIT.setting: Written after Paul's first imprisonment to Titus, whom he had left on Crete to set the young churches in order.
TIT.theme: Sound doctrine that produces good works
TIT.summary: Titus, a Gentile convert and trusted coworker, had been left on Crete to complete the organization of the churches there. Paul instructs him to ordain qualified elders, silence false teachers who were subverting whole houses, and teach each group in the church to adorn the doctrine of God by godly living. The letter grounds good works firmly in the grace of God, who saved us not by works of righteousness but according to His mercy.
TIT.christ: Jesus Christ is "the great God and our Saviour," who gave Himself to redeem us from all iniquity and purify a people zealous of good works.

outline.title: Ordaining elders and rebuking false teachers

PHM.author: the apostle Paul (with Timothy)
PHM.audience: Philemon of Colossae and the church in his house
PHM.setting: Written from Paul's first Roman imprisonment and sent with Onesimus alongside the letter to the Colossians.
PHM.summary: Onesimus, a slave who had run away from his master Philemon, came into contact with Paul in prison and was converted. Paul sends him back with this short personal letter, asking Philemon to receive him no longer merely as a servant but as a brother beloved. Paul offers to repay anything Onesimus owed, beautifully illustrating Christian forgiveness and the reconciling power of the gospel.
PHM.christ: Paul's plea to "put that on mine account" pictures Christ's work as Mediator, who takes our debt upon Himself and reconciles us to God.

outline.title: Thanksgiving for Philemon's love and faith

HEB.author: unknown (Paul, Apollos and others proposed)
HEB.audience: Jewish Christians tempted to turn back to Judaism
HEB.setting: Written before the temple's destruction in A.D. 70 to Hebrew believers under pressure to abandon Christ for the old covenant system.
HEB.theme: The superiority of Christ and the new covenant
HEB.summary: Hebrews was written to Jewish Christians who, under persecution and discouragement, were tempted to drift back to the Levitical system. The author, whose name is not given, shows that Jesus is superior to angels, Moses, and the Aaronic priests, and that His once-for-all sacrifice establishes a better covenant with better promises. Solemn warning passages and the great roll call of faith urge readers to hold fast, run with patience, and go forth unto Christ bearing His reproach.
HEB.christ: Christ is the Son through whom God has spoken in these last days, the brightness of His glory, and our great High Priest after the order of Melchizedek who offered Himself once for all.

outline.title: Christ superior to the prophets and angels
Christ superior to Moses; entering God's rest
Christ's priesthood after the order of Melchizedek
A better covenant, sanctuary, and sacrifice
Endurance, chastening, and the unshakable kingdom

JAS.author: James, the Lord's brother
JAS.setting: Probably among the earliest New Testament books, written from Jerusalem by a leader of the church there to Jewish Christians dispersed abroad and facing trials and poverty.
JAS.summary: James, the half-brother of Jesus who became a leader of the Jerusalem church, writes to the twelve tribes "scattered abroad." In a practical, proverb-like style reminiscent of the Sermon on the Mount, he addresses trials, the tongue, favoritism, worldliness, and the oppression of the poor by the rich. His central concern is that true saving faith is never mere profession but shows itself in obedience and good works.
JAS.christ: Jesus Christ is "the Lord of glory," whose coming draws nigh; His teaching echoes throughout the letter's call to be doers of the word.

outline.title: Hearers and doers of the word
Warning to the rich; patience and prayer

1PE.author: the apostle Peter
1PE.setting: Written from "Babylon" (most likely Rome) with Silvanus's help, as Christians faced slander and growing hostility for their faith.
1PE.theme: A living hope and holy living amid suffering
1PE.summary: Peter writes to believers scattered as strangers through the provinces of Asia Minor, who were suffering reproach and hostility for their faith. He reminds them of their lively hope through the resurrection, their identity as God's chosen generation and royal priesthood, and their call to holy living. He teaches them to submit to authorities, to suffer patiently as Christ did, and to humble themselves under God's mighty hand, who will exalt them in due time.
1PE.christ: Christ is the precious cornerstone and the suffering Servant who bare our sins in His own body on the tree, leaving us an example, and the chief Shepherd who will appear in glory.

outline.title: Called to holiness as God's people
Submission and good conduct among unbelievers

2PE.author: the apostle Peter
2PE.audience: the same believers addressed in 1 Peter
2PE.setting: Peter's final letter, written shortly before his martyrdom, as false teachers crept into the churches and scoffers denied the Lord's return.
2PE.theme: Grow in grace and knowledge; beware of false teachers
2PE.summary: Knowing his death was near, Peter wrote to stir up the memory of believers and guard them against false teachers. He calls them to add Christian virtues to their faith, grounds that faith in apostolic eyewitness testimony and the sure word of prophecy given by the Holy Spirit, and exposes the greed and immorality of the deceivers. He answers scoffers who denied the Lord's return, explaining that God's longsuffering leads to repentance and that the day of the Lord will surely come.
2PE.christ: Jesus Christ is our God and Saviour, whose majesty Peter saw on the holy mount, and the coming Lord whose day will bring new heavens and a new earth.

outline.title: The certainty of the Lord's coming

1JN.author: the apostle John
1JN.setting: Written late in the first century to churches shaken by teachers who had left them, denying that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.
1JN.theme: Fellowship with God and the assurance of eternal life
1JN.summary: John writes as an aged eyewitness to churches troubled by false teachers who had gone out from them, denying that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh while claiming to know God and living in sin. He sets out tests of true fellowship with God: believing the truth about Christ, keeping His commandments, and loving the brethren. His purpose is that believers' joy may be full and that they may know that they have eternal life.
1JN.christ: Jesus is the eternal Word of life who came in the flesh, our Advocate with the Father, and the propitiation for our sins.

outline.title: God is light: walking in fellowship
Children of God: righteousness and love
Trying the spirits; God is love

2JN.author: the apostle John ("the elder")
2JN.audience: "the elect lady and her children" (a Christian woman or a local church)
2JN.setting: Written late in the first century to warn against welcoming traveling teachers who denied that Christ had come in the flesh.
2JN.summary: In this brief note, "the elder" writes to "the elect lady and her children," either a Christian woman and her family or a local church. He rejoices that some are walking in truth, renews the commandment to love one another, and warns against deceivers who confess not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh. Believers must not receive or bid such teachers God speed, lest they share in their evil deeds.
2JN.christ: Jesus Christ is the Son of the Father, truly come in the flesh; whoever abides in His doctrine has both the Father and the Son.

3JN.author: the apostle John ("the elder")
3JN.audience: Gaius, a beloved and faithful believer
3JN.setting: Written late in the first century amid tension over receiving traveling missionaries, with John's authority opposed by Diotrephes.
3JN.summary: This personal letter from "the elder" to his beloved friend Gaius commends him for walking in the truth and for his hospitality to traveling brethren who went forth for Christ's name. John rebukes Diotrephes, who loved preeminence, refused to receive the brethren, and spoke maliciously against the apostle. He commends Demetrius and hopes to visit soon.
3JN.christ: Christ is not named directly, but the missionaries went forth "for his name's sake," and those who support them become fellowhelpers to the truth.

JUD.author: Jude, brother of James and of the Lord
JUD.audience: believers threatened by false teachers (recipients unspecified)
JUD.setting: Written in the later apostolic age to warn churches into which ungodly men had crept, turning grace into lasciviousness.
JUD.summary: Jude intended to write of the common salvation but felt compelled instead to exhort believers to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered unto the saints. Ungodly men had crept in unawares, turning the grace of God into lasciviousness and denying the Lord. Drawing on examples from the Old Testament and Jewish tradition, Jude shows their certain judgment, then exhorts the faithful to build themselves up, keep themselves in the love of God, and show compassion to the wavering.
JUD.christ: Jesus Christ is the Lord whom the apostates deny, in whom believers are preserved, and whose mercy they look for unto eternal life.

outline.title: The certain judgment of the ungodly

REV.author: the apostle John
REV.setting: Written while John was exiled on Patmos, traditionally under the emperor Domitian, as the churches faced persecution, false teaching, and pressure to compromise.
REV.theme: The triumph of the Lamb and the coming of His kingdom
REV.summary: While on Patmos "for the word of God," John received the Revelation of Jesus Christ and was commanded to write it to seven churches in Asia. After messages of commendation and warning to those churches, he sees visions of God's throne and the Lamb, judgments unfolding through seals, trumpets, and vials, and the conflict between Christ and Satan with his beasts. The book climaxes with Christ's return, the binding of Satan, the final judgment, and the new heaven and new earth, assuring suffering believers that the Lamb shall overcome.
REV.christ: Jesus Christ is the faithful witness and glorified Son of man, the Lamb that was slain and is worthy, and the King of kings who comes to judge and reign for ever.

outline.title: Prologue and vision of the glorified Christ
The throne in heaven and the Lamb
The woman, the dragon, and the beasts
The seven vials and the fall of Babylon
Christ's return, the thousand years, and final judgment
New heaven and new earth; epilogue
